title: Your eyes don’t glide over a scene: they jump two or three times a second

cover.alt: Black-and-white infrared close-up of a single eye: grey iris, round black pupil, two small white reflections and the lashes above.

body: When you look at a picture or read, your eyes don’t sweep smoothly. They make quick jumps called **saccades**, from the French for ‘jerk’, stopping on one spot after another, two or three times a second. The reason is the **fovea**, the sharp-seeing centre of the retina: it covers only about 1–2 degrees of your view, so your eyes keep aiming it at new details, and your brain stitches the glimpses into one steady scene.

slides.alt: Black-and-white infrared close-up of an eye. The iris and pupil hold still, then flick to a new position, again and again, while the pupil slowly changes size.
slides.caption: An infrared camera in a lab in Tübingen, Germany, films one eye as a volunteer looks freely at a picture. The eye holds still, jumps and holds still again, while the pupil widens and narrows.

slides.prompt: Stand at a mirror and look from one of your eyes to the other. What do you see?
slides.answer: Your eyes never seem to move
slides.detail: A friend watching would see them jump. During each jump, or saccade, your brain hides the movement, an effect called saccadic masking, and even hides that anything was hidden.

slides.label: how long a typical saccade lasts while you read
slides.text: Bigger jumps take up to about 200 ms. Reacting to something unexpected takes around 200 ms before the eyes even start to move.

slides.heading: How fast a saccade can turn the eye, at its peak
slides.note: Peak speeds for large saccades. Blinks can be faster still.

slides.heading: Spotted with a mirror
slides.text: The word seems to have been coined in the 1870s by the French eye doctor Émile Javal. He put a mirror beside a page to watch people reading silently, and saw that their eyes moved in a string of separate jumps, not one smooth sweep.

slides.question: Why do your eyes keep jumping from spot to spot?
options: Only a tiny patch sees sharply
To stop the eyes drying out
slides.explanation: The fovea, the retina’s sharp centre, covers only about 1–2 degrees of view, so the eyes aim it at one detail after another.
